content: The term somatic pertains to the body, distinguishing it from other entities such as the mind. The word originates from the Greek term Σωματικός (Somatikòs), which translates to of the body. Its meaning varies across different fields of study. In neurobiology, somatic is used as an adjective to describe the soma, which is the part of a neuron that contains the cell nucleus. In anatomy, the term refers to the portion of the nervous system responsible for voluntary movements and sensory perception, as well as the ability to assess relative effort and weight, a function known as proprioception. Somatic muscles, in this context, are those associated with the musculoskeletal system. In genetics, somatic refers to cells or tissues that are not part of the germline. For instance, somatic mutations occur in non-reproductive cells and, in animals, cannot be passed on to offspring. In the philosophy of education, certain concepts related to the body and mind are referred to as somatics. According to the originator of this usage, somatic awareness enables individuals to derive wisdom from within themselves. Thomas Hanna's interpretation of somatic emphasizes a fully integrated nature of the mind, body, and spirit in humans. However, the broader, popular understanding of the term has not yet fully embraced this integrated perspective, and a dualistic view of the mind and body often persists, even in disciplines that describe themselves as somatic. The related term soma refers to the entire axial portion of an animal, which includes the head, neck, trunk, and tail.
